subtitle: Why files were not enough, how a database hides storage details, and how to draw the world before building tables.

why.body:
Picture a university where the exams office, the library and the hostel each keep their own file of students. A student changes her phone number at the library, and the exams office never hears about it. Which number is right? Nobody knows, and that small mess is why databases exist.

Storing data in separate files per application leads to redundancy (the same fact stored many times), inconsistency (two copies disagree), no sharing or concurrent safety, and code tied to file formats. A DBMS keeps data in one place and provides a query language, integrity rules, concurrent access, security and recovery after failure. You already depend on them: banking, airline reservation, universities, web sites. What does a DBMS mainly solve? Redundancy and inconsistency, in one stroke.
keynotes: File-based storage leads to redundancy, inconsistency (two copies disagree), no sharing or concurrent safety, and code tied to file formats.
A DBMS keeps data in one place and provides a query language, integrity rules, concurrent access, security and recovery after failure.
Applications include banking, airline reservation, universities and web sites.

abs.body:
When you drive a car, you do not think about pistons. A good database works the same way: it hides the engine behind three levels of abstraction. The physical level describes how records are stored (files, indexes). The logical level describes what data exists and the relationships between them (tables). The view level shows each user only the part they need.

Why is this wonderful? Because of two kinds of independence. Physical data independence: you can change the storage layout without changing the logical schema. Logical data independence: you can change the schema without rewriting every view or application. A schema is the design; an instance is the data at this moment. So adding an index without changing any query is an example of physical data independence. Each level hides the one below, as the figure shows.
keynotes: The physical level describes how records are stored, the logical level what data exists and its relationships, and the view level shows each user only what they need.
Physical data independence changes storage without changing the logical schema; logical data independence changes the schema without rewriting views or applications.
A schema is the design; an instance is the data at this moment.

er.body:
Before building tables, an architect draws a plan, and so should you. The entity–relationship model is that plan for data. An entity is a distinguishable thing (Student, Course); an entity set is a collection of them. Attributes describe entities, and a key attribute uniquely identifies one (studentID). Composite, multivalued and derived attributes also exist.

Things relate to each other. A relationship associates entities (Student enrols in Course) with a cardinality: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. Students enrol in many courses and each course has many students, so that relationship is many-to-many. And a weak entity has no key of its own and depends on an owner (Dependent of Employee). Notice in the figure how a many-to-many relationship becomes a third box with two one-to-many links.
keynotes: An entity is a distinguishable thing (Student, Course); attributes describe it and a key attribute uniquely identifies one.
A relationship associates entities with a cardinality: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many.
A weak entity has no key of its own and depends on an owner, like Dependent of Employee.

gen.body:
Real worlds have hierarchies: a Student is a Person, a Teacher is an Employee. The extended ER model captures that. Specialisation splits an entity set into subclasses (Employee → Teacher, Clerk) which inherit attributes; generalisation is the same idea seen bottom-up. Aggregation treats a relationship as an entity so it can take part in another relationship.

You choose the rules with two questions: are the subclasses disjoint or overlapping, and is participation total or partial? If a Student “is a” Person, the Student inherits all of the Person’s attributes, as the figure shows.
keynotes: Specialisation splits an entity set into subclasses that inherit attributes; generalisation is the same idea bottom-up.
Aggregation treats a relationship as an entity so it can take part in another relationship.
Constraints: disjoint versus overlapping, total versus partial participation.

map.body:
Time to turn the drawing into real tables. The rules are few, and you will use them all your life. Each strong entity becomes a table (key = primary key). A one-to-many relationship puts the “one” side’s key into the “many” table as a foreign key. A many-to-many relationship becomes its own table whose primary key is the pair of foreign keys, plus the relationship’s attributes. A weak entity’s table includes the owner’s key in its key.

Apply them. Student(id, name) and Course(code, title) with a many-to-many “enrols with grade” become three tables: Student(id, name), Course(code, title), and Enrolment(id → Student, code → Course, grade), with primary key (id, code). In a one-to-many relationship, the foreign key goes in the table on the “many” side.
keynotes: Each strong entity becomes a table whose key is the primary key.
A one-to-many relationship puts the “one” side’s key into the “many” table as a foreign key.
A many-to-many relationship becomes its own table whose primary key is the pair of foreign keys: Enrolment(id, code, grade).

keys.body:
How does a database tell two rows apart? You need keys, and there is a small family of them. A superkey is any set of attributes that identifies a row. A candidate key is a minimal superkey, one with nothing to spare. The primary key is the candidate chosen, and a foreign key references another table’s key.

Two golden rules guard the keys. Entity integrity: a primary key is never null. Referential integrity: a foreign key matches an existing key or is null. A candidate key is a superkey from which no attribute can be removed.
keynotes: A superkey is any set of attributes that identifies a row; a candidate key is a minimal superkey; the primary key is the candidate chosen.
A foreign key references another table’s key.
Entity integrity: a primary key is never null; referential integrity: a foreign key matches an existing key or is null.
